question: Which description best captures the route to an operating facility?
correct: Needs and feasibility feed design and delivery; verification and handover connect the result to operation, with feedback between stages.
wrong: Construction starts, then the owner defines performance needs.
Needs should shape design and delivery rather than wait for construction.
Every stage finishes permanently before any other stage can begin.
Work overlaps and changed assumptions can require revisiting earlier decisions.

question: What does early commissioning planning contribute?
correct: It connects intended outcomes to a design that can be verified and handed into operation.
wrong: It removes the need for later testing.
Planning defines how later evidence will be obtained; it does not replace that evidence.
It is mainly a certificate produced after all installation is complete.
Commissioning thinking can influence design, testing and the operational transition.

question: The structure is progressing while utility engineering continues. What does that tell you?
correct: The workstreams have different milestones and must converge at service readiness.
wrong: Structural progress establishes that power will be ready.
Progress in one workstream is not evidence of service readiness in another.
All building work must be stopped until every utility task is complete.
The question establishes a dependency, not a universal rule stopping all parallel work.

question: An owner's expected use changes during design. What is the sound response?
correct: Reassess assumptions and carry agreed changes into the design and verification criteria.
wrong: Keep earlier performance assumptions because the phase has already started.
A phase boundary does not eliminate changed requirements.
Change one drawing and leave the test criteria alone.
Agreed changes need to propagate through the affected design and verification information.

question: What is a useful first view of site suitability?
correct: Power, connectivity, cooling resources, expansion space and site constraints all need consideration.
wrong: Enough land means the main suitability question is settled.
A parcel still needs the infrastructure and conditions to support the intended facility.
Every data center requires exactly the same water and network arrangement.
Cooling and connectivity needs depend on the proposed facility.

question: Why can the lowest purchase price be a poor site choice?
correct: Infrastructure constraints and whole-life operating suitability can outweigh a cheap land price.
wrong: Land price is the only cost set by site selection.
Site choice also shapes delivery, resilience, expansion and operation.
Operating costs can always be fixed later without changing the facility.
Site constraints can persist through the facility's life.

question: A substation is nearby. What further evidence is needed?
correct: Required capacity, connection work and service arrangements supporting the intended readiness date.
wrong: A short physical distance proves an opening-date connection.
Proximity does not establish capacity, engineering or delivery readiness.
A similar neighboring project's connection date is sufficient.
Another project's date does not establish this project's connection arrangements.

question: Equal-area sites have different water and fiber access. How should you compare them?
correct: Assess cooling/resource fit and network/infrastructure fit for the intended facility.
wrong: Treat them as equivalent because area is unchanged.
Area alone says little about external infrastructure suitability.
Reject every site with less water regardless of its cooling design.
Cooling technology and the intended operating needs affect resource requirements.

question: Which distinction between UPS and generator is useful at this level?
correct: UPS supports short interruptions and disturbances; designed generator backup can cover a longer normal-supply loss.
wrong: A UPS and generator have identical functions and transfer behavior.
They address related but different parts of continuity; arrangements vary.
A generator makes any short-interruption support unnecessary.
A longer-duration backup role does not establish uninterrupted support during transfer.

question: Why include cooling in power-continuity thinking?
correct: Cooling equipment has electrical dependencies, so assess continuity of the combined supporting system.
wrong: Energized IT proves cooling will remain available.
Pumps, fans and related supporting equipment also depend on electricity.
Cooling and electrical systems can always be assessed independently.
Their interfaces matter to facility operation.

question: Adequate cooling capacity exists but units respond inconsistently. What should you examine?
correct: Controls, sensors and coordinated response to load and conditions.
wrong: Capacity ratings prove the controls must work correctly.
Available capacity and coordinated operating behavior are different questions.
More nominal capacity is necessarily the only remedy.
The stated symptom may involve control or coordination rather than capacity.

question: Planned IT load rises sharply without a footprint change. What should be reassessed?
correct: Electrical and cooling capacity against the revised load and its distribution.
wrong: No infrastructure assumptions change if floor area stays fixed.
IT demand, not floor area alone, drives supporting requirements.
Only the number of racks matters; cooling and power can stay fixed.
Both electrical and thermal demand may change.

question: Which role map is the most useful starting point?
correct: Owner: requirements and acceptance; designers: solution; contractors: delivery; commissioning provider: verification coordination.
wrong: The commissioning provider automatically designs and installs every system.
Coordinating verification does not transfer all design and delivery responsibilities.
Once design begins, the owner no longer contributes requirements or acceptance.
Owner goals and acceptance remain part of the delivery process.

question: How do OPR and BOD relate?
correct: OPR describes needed outcomes and criteria; BOD explains the technical design response.
wrong: OPR is the installer's record drawing; BOD is a test certificate.
Those are different information needs; OPR and BOD connect requirements and design.
Both describe only the owner's business goals with no technical response.
The BOD sets out the design team's technical approach.

question: A commissioning reviewer finds a design issue. What follows?
correct: Route it to the responsible party, then resolve and verify through the agreed process.
wrong: Finding it automatically makes the reviewer responsible for redesign and installation.
Finding an issue does not transfer every delivery responsibility.
No one needs to track it because the reviewer is not the designer.
Role boundaries still require an issue-resolution and verification route.

question: A team agrees a cooling-equipment change. What handoff matters next?
correct: Check affected interfaces and coordinate current requirements with the relevant design, installation and site teams.
wrong: Only the team making the change needs the revised information.
A local change can invalidate another team's assumptions.
Install to the older details and update information only at handover.
Affected work needs current coordinated information before it continues.

question: What is the purpose of a product-data or shop-drawing submittal?
correct: Present proposed delivery details for the required review against project requirements.
wrong: Automatically rewrite the contract without a separate change route.
Submittal review and an authorized requirement change are different processes in the cited context.
Replace every design requirement with the supplier's normal product.
The proposed details must be reviewed against the applicable requirements.

question: Why allow review time before fabrication and delivery?
correct: Review and coordination are upstream dependencies of usable delivery commitments.
wrong: An equipment arrival date captures all prior decisions.
It hides the review and fabrication dependencies.
Every project uses one universal submittal-review duration.
Plan the sequence for the project; the source establishes no universal duration.

question: A proposed substitution deviates from a requirement. What should happen?
correct: Make the deviation explicit and use the authorized clarification or change process.
wrong: Ordinary submittal review always changes the agreed requirement.
The cited contract-form context distinguishes submittals from contract changes.
Leave the deviation unstated if the replacement looks similar.
Affected requirements and interfaces need an explicit reviewed decision.

question: Why document a changed concealed service route?
correct: Preserve significant installed changes in controlled records for future users.
wrong: A verbal update is durable enough for future maintenance teams.
Hidden work becomes difficult to reconstruct and team knowledge can be lost.
Record drawings are automatically exact surveys of every installed detail.
Their accuracy and responsibility need to be defined; do not assume that guarantee.

question: All components pass individual start-up checks. What is still unproven?
correct: Their combined interactions and performance under the facility's intended conditions.
wrong: Individual passes establish the integrated system's performance.
Interfaces and control responses can fail even when components work alone.
No evidence of any component function exists yet.
The individual checks provide component evidence; the missing evidence concerns the combined system.

question: Why distinguish functional checks, integrated tests and operational transition?
correct: They answer different readiness questions, including whether people can take the facility into operation.
wrong: One passing test necessarily answers all readiness questions.
Equipment function, combined behavior and transition needs can expose different gaps.
Every provider uses identical numbered commissioning stages.
Framework names and numbers vary; learn their purposes.

question: A passed factory test is presented as completed site acceptance. What remains?
correct: Evidence of post-delivery condition, correct installation and required on-site and integrated operation.
wrong: Factory evidence proves nothing could change during shipping or installation.
The factory test does not observe those later stages.
Every factory test must be ignored because only site results matter.
Factory evidence is useful, but it does not substitute for the required site evidence.

question: Operations has a test certificate but lacks training and useful system information. What is missing?
correct: An operating handoff with current system information, procedures, verification/issue records, maintenance information and training.
wrong: Nothing; a passing certificate contains all operating knowledge.
A test result alone does not preserve how the delivered facility is understood and operated.
Only a list of supplier names is needed for operational readiness.
Useful system information, training, procedures and records remain necessary handoff needs.
